extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemaking officials, administrative law scholars, policymakers, and practitioners involved in notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for agencies on identifying, evaluating, and responding to mass, malattributed, and computer-generated public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking, covering legal obligations, policy tradeoffs, and technological and procedural remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice content requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice shall include a statement of the time, place, and nature of public rule making proceedings; reference to the legal authority under which the rule is proposed; and either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require agencies to disclose scientific or technical details on which they base proposed rules so the public has a fair opportunity to react; adequate notice facilitates meaningful comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to participate and consideration obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: After notice, the agency shall give interested persons an opportunity to participate through submission of written data, views, or arguments and, after consideration of the relevant matter presented, incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose (5 U.S.C. § 553(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Person’ is broadly defined and courts construe participation expansively. Agencies must consider relevant matters presented in comments; this underpins later obligations to respond to significant points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must respond in the notice of final rule to ‘significant’ comments—those that, if true, would require a change in the proposed rule—failure to do so can be grounds for remand under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard (e.g., Am. Mining Cong. v. EPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A response is required when comments raise substantive concerns; but the responsiveness requirement is subject to a commonsense exception for speculative comments without factual/policy basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense exception to responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that are purely speculative and do not disclose the factual or policy basis on which they rest require no response (Nat. Res. Def. Council v. EPA; Home Box Off. v. FCC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may decline lengthy responses to comments lacking factual basis; courts recognize limits to required responsiveness to avoid burdensome obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a mass comment response/campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A ‘mass comment response’ is an unusually large number of comments for a rulemaking (generally at least an order-of-magnitude, e.g., 10x, above a typical level for that agency); a ‘mass comment campaign’ is a special case where one or more organizations has urged many individuals to submit comments or submitted comments in their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No rigid numeric threshold is prescribed; the appropriate threshold varies by agency and rule; identification involves agency-specific baselines and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Malattributed’ comments are comments falsely attributed to persons by whom they were not in fact submitted (submitted under false names or identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution can be facilitated by easy access to large data sets (e.g., DMV or voter files) and automation; the term is preferred here to the more colloquial ‘fraudulent’ or ‘fake’ when the specific problem is incorrect commenter identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Computer-generated comments’ are those generated by a software algorithm that replaces human content generation, so that once automated the software can submit comments (possibly repeatedly) without further human engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary NLP models can produce human‑like text; while past automated comments were crude cut-and-pastes, advanced models (e.g., GPT-3) create harder-to-detect, seemingly unique submissions, raising risk of scale and quality issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess public comments for information quality: accuracy, uniqueness, presence of false statements or deceptive attributions, and whether comments provide substantive data, views, or arguments relevant to the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low information quality (duplicative content, false identities, automated gibberish) reduces utility of the docket and increases burden on agency staff; agencies should focus responses on comments that supply substantive, fact-based inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and perceived integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how comment submissions affect the legitimacy and public perception of the rulemaking process—whether mass, malattributed, or automated submissions undermine trust or create a perception of manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not legally dispositive, large-scale or inauthentic submissions can erode perceived legitimacy; agencies should consider reputational effects and steps to preserve public confidence (transparency about handling and any findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing costs and resource burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the processing costs of high-volume, duplicative, malattributed, or automated comments—including staff time to sort, de-duplicate, summarize, and respond to submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should weigh cost of manual review versus adoption of technological tools (de‑duplication, clustering, summarization) and design procedures that make review tractable without impairing meaningful consideration of substantive inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of mass, malattributed, and automated comments under law
rubrics_metrics.description: There is generally no legal prohibition against receiving mass comments, and malattributed or computer-generated comments do not typically violate federal law except in extreme circumstances (some instances may implicate fraud or false-statement statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should not reflexively treat such comments as invalid; legal action or setting aside a rule based solely on mass/automated/malattributed comments is unlikely except where statutory crimes or other legal violations are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal and statutory responses to malattribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments may implicate criminal prohibitions (e.g., fraud, making false statements) in certain instances; agencies should be aware of legal thresholds for referral or enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While criminal statutes may apply in egregious cases, routine malattribution typically does not trigger criminal sanctions; agencies should coordinate with counsel and consider proportional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligations regarding acceptance, cleansing, and reliance on malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal issues include whether agencies have an obligation to accept and consider malattributed comments, whether they must ‘cleanse’ the docket of such comments, and guidance on whether agencies may rely on malattributed input when making decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have addressed responsiveness obligations but do not impose a broad duty to remove every malattributed comment; agencies should document how they treat questionable submissions and avoid reliance on potentially misleading evidence of public support without careful vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and publicize comment-handling policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt and publish policies that encourage helpful, substantive comments and discourage or prohibit misleading submissions (e.g., policies on duplicate submissions, format, or provenance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, public policies (rather than secret or ad hoc practices) help set expectations for commenters and provide accountability for how agencies treat mass or questionable comments; policies should balance access with integrity and be explained in rule preambles or guidance materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt technological tools for screening and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should take advantage of available software tools that can screen, sort, de-duplicate, cluster, summarize, and digest large volumes of submissions to reduce burden and enhance insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of algorithms and summarization technologies can surface substantive themes and reduce staff time; agencies should transparently document methods and limitations, and combine automated processing with human review for important or contested issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer policy/technology remedies and more speech to punitive enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The recommended institutional response to abuses is modest: develop procedures and technical solutions rather than relying primarily on criminal prosecution or setting aside rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses should be proportionate; emphasize improving processes (screening, better public engagement mechanisms, transparent handling) and use ‘more speech’ (e.g., publicizing findings, soliciting clarifying input) rather than heavy-handed enforcement except in egregious cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative and enhanced participation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should explore alternative engagement methods (summarization tools, representative mini-publics, citizen juries/assemblies, collaborative drafting, wiki surveys, evidence checks) to elicit higher-quality, more legible, and more legitimate input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods can produce more deliberative, expert, or representative inputs and can complement traditional rulemaking comments; agencies should pilot and evaluate such innovations to increase meaningful participation and reduce vulnerability to mass/automated manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: E‑rulemaking infrastructure and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Post required materials online, maintain accessible rulemaking dockets (e.g., Regulations.gov), and facilitate electronic submission to broaden participation and provide transparency about materials on which a proposed rule is based (E-Government Act obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online dockets increase access and transparency but also enable new pathologies; agencies should ensure infrastructure supports analysis tools, metadata capture (e.g., provenance), and public explanation of how comments are processed.
